newsitem.title: FRANCE: Outlawed Islamist FIS condemns killings in Algeria.
newsitem.headline: Outlawed Islamist FIS condemns killings in Algeria.

text.p: Algeria's banned Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) leadership denounced the latest surge of bloodshed in Algeria ahead of Friday mass prayers, marked in the last two weeks by two car bombs which killed more than 20 people.

"Algeria experienced a frightening escalation of blind terrorism in the last two weeks.... We condemn with force these criminal acts," said the Europe-based FIS executive committee leadership in a statement faxed on Thursday to news organisations in Paris.

The statement said more than 90 civilians had been killed in the past two weeks. The FIS leadership has tried to distance itself from radical guerrillas whom Algerian authorities blame for the killings.
These included the slaying, earlier this month, of more than 30 travellers in the southern region of Laghouat.
The FIS leadership urged the international community to voice concern at the increased violence in Algeria.

"In the face of this painful situation experienced by the Algerian people, which claims more than 120,000 victims, it would be indecent that the international community keeps silent like a plotter-witness to this dreadful tragedy," it said.

Legal secular opposition groups in Algeria put the figure of those killed in nearly five years of violence at 70,000. Western intelligence and independent sources say more than 50,000 people have died.
The FIS leadership sees the increased violence as a consequence of the Algerian authorities' failure to talk with outlawed fundamentalist leaders.
"Instead of negotiating with the FIS to end the country's crisis, the authorities preferred a fake dialogue to fool the public opinion at home and abroad," it added.

President Liamine Zeroual, who wound up talks with legal opposition parties last month by sealing a reform pact with 38 party and union leaders, including two Islamist groups, this week set November 28 as the date for a referendum to amend the constitution.

The proposed changes would underline the Moslem faith as the religion of the Algerian state, lay the ground for the banning of Islamist parties, and forbid violence-oriented parties from seeking power.
Algeria erupted in violence shortly after authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election in which the FIS had taken a commanding lead.
